messages.body_plain:
Dear Richard,

so I ran a small simulation study (with 100 rep data sets) on the DM-Nmix model with full time-dependence in the parameters absent a robust design. Here are the descriptors of the data sets (I varied all params quite considerably): M = 50, T = 5, lambda = 2, gamma = c(0.5, 1, 0.5, 1), omega = c(0.6, 0.9, 0.6, 0.9), p = c(0.6, 0.8, 0.6, 0.8, 0.6).

Here is a summary of the estimates from the 100 simreps, with the last two columns the mean and the sd over the 100 estimates. The raw estimate is the mean count in the first year (-99.0 denote NAs).

> print(cbind(ss1, ss2), dig = 3)
                            TRUTH Raw esti DM Esti   ss2
Mean abundance (lambda)       2.0      1.2   2.220 0.523
Recruitment (gamma 1)         0.5    -99.0   0.410 0.505
Recruitment (gamma 2)         1.0    -99.0   0.841 0.514
Recruitment (gamma 3)         0.5    -99.0   0.644 0.442
Recruitment (gamma 4)         1.0    -99.0   0.824 0.551
Survival (omega 1)            0.6    -99.0   0.633 0.174
Survival (omega 2)            0.9    -99.0   0.858 0.162
Survival (omega 3)            0.6    -99.0   0.653 0.171
Survival (omega 4)            0.9    -99.0   0.827 0.156
Detection probability (p 1)   0.6    -99.0   0.564 0.136
Detection probability (p 2)   0.8    -99.0   0.794 0.184
Detection probability (p 3)   0.6    -99.0   0.675 0.161
Detection probability (p 4)   0.8    -99.0   0.788 0.179
Detection probability (p 5)   0.6    -99.0   0.664 0.147

>From this, I would tentatively conclude that the params are identifiable even with full time-dependence and no RD, but that the estimates are probably rather crappy. From looking at the variability among the 100 data sets (i.e., the sd in the last column), it appears that the colonization params are particularly shaky.

This is a first stab only, and over the next months or so I'd be interested to look more into the capabilities of the model for particular data formats. More on that later.

Thanks a lot for providing such conventient code for the DM Nmix model in unmarked !

Kind regards  -- Marc

Hi Marc,

It would be rather cruel if it was that difficult. Fortunately, you just need to create one M X T matrix and supply it as a yearlySiteCov. Continuing with the example on the help page, try this:

year <- matrix(as.character(1:5), 50, 5, byrow=TRUE)
umf <- unmarkedFramePCO(y=y, yearlySiteCovs=list(year=year), numPrimary=5)
m2 <- pcountOpen(~1, ~year, ~year, ~year, umf, K=20, control=list(trace=TRUE, REPORT=1)) # K should be higher

On a separate note, I wonder if the parameters are identifiable in this case. It shouldn't be a problem if you have "robust design" data, but I would suggest doing some simulations to check out the properties of the model when you have year-specific gamma/omega/p and no secondary samples. If you do look into this, please let us know what you find. And if you are interested in some simulation code, there are several simulation tests in a the file that comes with unmarked:  /R/library/unmarked/inst/unitTests/sim.pcountOpen.R, which is also here: https://github.com/rbchan/unmarked/blob/master/inst/unitTests/sim.pcountOpen.r .

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

Your results don't look as bad as I expected, but like you say, they aren't great either. I will continue to play devil's advocate because it goes against my intuition that the parameters could be identifiable in this case. My understanding is that p is only identifiable because of the constraints placed upon the population dynamics. For example, when gamma and omega don't vary (are scalars), the population should reach equilibrium rather quickly. Deviations from this would be information about detection probability. But if gamma and omega are year-specific, then the population dynamics are nearly unconstrained, so it's hard to see where information about p could come from (unless you had RD data). But this is just my intuition... which is often wrong.

I guess the problem is that it is very hard to demonstrate identifiability.  If you do pursue this some more, it might be worth checking to see how often the hessian can be inverted (do you get SEs if se=TRUE), and how sensitive the estimates are to starting values. And maybe David Dail would be worth contacting to see if he has looked into this.

It would be great to get to the bottom of this so that we can block certain models from being fitted if need be. Thanks so much for working on this -- the properties of this model need more study.

Richard

Hi Pablo,

The likelihood of your data at the starting values is 0, so the log-likelihood is -Inf. You could try other starting values, but I think there is another problem here. I will continue to play devil's advocate because it goes against my intuition that the parameters could be identifiable in this case. My understanding is that p is only identifiable because of the constraints placed upon the population dynamics. But if gamma and omega are year-specific, then the population dynamics are nearly unconstrained, so it's hard to see where information about p could come from (unless you had RD data). But this is just my intuition... which is often wrong.

I guess the problem is that it is very hard to demonstrate identifiability. extinct within a year.  The model fm <- colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~occasion,

messages.body_plain:
Manuel,

Even though there is no interaction, there are still 9 possible predicted values.  Since there is no interaction, these 9 predicted values each are a sum of only two estimates.  Predict is just adding the estimates as you would expect from the newData object that you printed.  So all is well there.

I have a feeling that what you want is more like a marginal prediction (like SAS's LSMEANS), where you get the predicted value for each level of one factor, averaged over the levels of the other factor (see for example http://www.uiweb.uidaho.edu/ag/statprog/sas/workshops/glm/handout2.1_glm.pdf).  You would need to compute these manually since unmarked/R doesn't have an LSMEANS equivalent that I'm aware of.  You might make use of unmarked's linearComb method to help you out.

Ian

Hi Manuel,

Andy is exactly right -- this will give you the point estimates for the LSMEANS.  And if you additionally want to get the standard errors, then linearComb will provide this for you.  To help you figure out the coefficients to use with linearComb, here's a small reproducible example using lm (since this is an R modeling issue rather than an unmarked issue).

> data <- data.frame(f1 = gl(3, 3, 27, c("a", "b", "c")),
>                    f2 = gl(3, 1, 27,  c("a", "b", "c")),
>                    y = rnorm(27))
> fm <- lm(y ~ f1 + f2, data)
> coef(fm)
> (Intercept)         f1b         f1c         f2b         f2c
>  0.06979306 -0.18754312  0.56563158 -0.46392095 -0.26595500

Then, you would get your LSMEANS with the following 6 vectors.

> f1,f2, coefficients
> a, .:  1,0,0,1/3,1/3
> b, .:  1,1,0,1/3,1/3
> c, .:  1,0,1,1/3,1/3
> ., a:  1,1/3,1/3,0,0
> ., b:  1,1/3,1/3,1,0
> ., c:  1,1/3,1/3,0,1

You can make these into a single matrix and pass it to linearComb.

Hope that helps,
Ian

Hi Jason,

Thanks for posting the reproducible example. unmarked doesn't try to select smart starting values, so sometimes you need to look at your data and make an educated guess. The log of the counts in year1 is 2.4, so starting at 3 makes sense, and this works:

smbmod1<-pcountOpen(~1,~1,~1,~1,smbf,mixture="P",K=150,
                    starts=c(3,0,0,0))

However, this gives similar results to what you found with the negative binomial model, and so you will probably think that abundance is too high. The reason for the high estimate of abundance is that there is extreme variation in the counts for some sites but not others,

matplot(t(smb), type="b")

and you have no covariates in the model to explain this variation (which may be due to actual abundance or detection). Without covariates, and given the assumed state model, the evidence points to low detection probability. Also, without covariates, your model will probably not pass a goodness-of-fit test.

Richard

year and one's that don't would be one way of inferring whether the
occupancy is changing over time.

Hi Whitney,

Thanks for the link. I didn't know about user-defined contrasts.

The issue that you face now is that your estimate of psi is near a parameter boundary, ie psi is very close to 1. This makes it hard to find the MLEs of the and obtain SEs from the hessian.

You could try a few different things.

1. Use starting values and play around with some of optim()'s control arguments. See ?optim.

m <- occu(~1 ~1, sesp.occu, starts=c(5, 2), control=list(rel.tol=1e-30))

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Temporal trends in occupancy
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jorge,

One problem with using single-season occupancy models to model multi-season data is that you are ignoring the serial correlation within sites among seasons. Put another way, the model would be assuming that you have a new random sample of sites each year, which you do not. This could lead to artificially small estimates of variance, but on the other hand, it is probably a reasonable place to begin.

The other option is to formally recognize the serial correlation using the MacKenzie et al. (2003) model, which can be implemented using colext. Trend is not a parameter per se, but you could compute it as a derived parameter. See

vignette("colext")

for more details. It is also possible to reformulate the MacKenzie et al. (2003) model so that you are modeling occupancy probability each year, instead of colonization and extinction. That might be another way of estimating trend, but that parameterization is not implemented in unmarked. I think it is in PRESENCE though. Regardless, I agree with Hardin that a multi-season model would probably be more appropriate here.

Richard
